chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Ahmad ibn A'sham from Mansur ibn Hazim said: Ahmad ibn al-Nu'man asked him.
He said: 'Do I pray while in my litter (sedan chair) while I am ill?' He said, so he said: 'As for the voluntary prayer, yes; and as for the obligatory prayer, no.'

He said: And Ahmad mentioned the severity of his ailment, so he said: 'I was severely ill, so I would order them, when the prayer time arrived, to lower me (from the litter), so I would be carried on my bedding, placed down, and I would pray. Then I would be carried on my bedding, placed down, and put back into my litter.'
Because this report is construed as recommending (voluntary prayer) rather than obligatory (prayer), and to add clarification to what we said is what was narrated:

key_terms.مَحْمِلِي: litter or sedan chair (a seat carried by servants)

ai.seo_question: Can a severely ill person pray obligatory prayers while sitting in a litter or sedan chair?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq clarifies the fiqh of the severely ill (*al-mudtir*) by distinguishing between voluntary (*nafl*) and obligatory (*fard*) prayers. While voluntary prayers may be performed while remaining in the litter, obligatory prayers require the individual to be lowered to the ground to ensure the proper execution of movements, a ruling supported by the narrator’s personal experience of being carried out for prayer and returned. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly principle that ease (*rukhas*) does not negate the requirement for the essential pillars of obligatory worship when physically feasible.
